questions.question_en: According to von Thünen's concentric rings around the central city in 'Der Isolierte Staat', why is 'Forestry (Firewood and Lumber)' located in the SECOND ring closer to the city than extensive grain farming?
questions.question_hi:
[Unit 1: Agricultural Regions & Models]
According to von Thünen's concentric rings around the central city in 'Der Isolierte Staat', why is 'Forestry (Firewood and Lumber)' located in the SECOND ring closer to the city than extensive grain farming?
options_en: In 19th-century Europe, wood was the primary fuel and building material, and its extreme bulk/weight made wagon transport costs prohibitive over long distances
Trees required more fertile alluvial soil than wheat
Forestry needed daily irrigation from urban canals
Grain crops could only grow in arid outer fringes
options_hi: In 19th-century Europe, wood was the primary fuel and building material, and its extreme bulk/weight made wagon transport costs prohibitive over long distances
Trees required more fertile alluvial soil than wheat
Forestry needed daily irrigation from urban canals
Grain crops could only grow in arid outer fringes
questions.explanation_en: Because wood was bulky, heavy, and in high demand for fuel and construction in 1826, its transport cost per hectare of output (Y·F) was steep, giving forestry a steeper bid-rent curve near the market than grain.

आधिकारिक व्याख्या (Unit 1: Agricultural Regions & Models):
Because wood was bulky, heavy, and in high demand for fuel and construction in 1826, its transport cost per hectare of output (Y·F) was steep, giving forestry a steeper bid-rent curve near the market than grain.

questions.question_en: In Alfred Weber's (1909) Least-Cost Theory of Industrial Location, the 'Material Index' (MI) is defined as the ratio of:
questions.question_hi:
[Unit 2: Industrial Location Theories]
In Alfred Weber's (1909) Least-Cost Theory of Industrial Location, the 'Material Index' (MI) is defined as the ratio of:
options_en: Weight of localized (weight-losing) raw materials to the weight of the finished product
Weight of ubiquities (water/air) to total labor cost
Transport cost of finished goods to agglomeration savings
Total capital investment to weight of raw materials
options_hi: Weight of localized (weight-losing) raw materials to the weight of the finished product
Weight of ubiquities (water/air) to total labor cost
Transport cost of finished goods to agglomeration savings
Total capital investment to weight of raw materials
questions.explanation_en: Weber defined Material Index MI = (Weight of localized raw materials) / (Weight of finished product). If MI > 1 (weight-losing industry like iron smelting or sugar milling), the optimal plant location is pulled toward the raw material source; if MI ≤ 1, it locates at the market.
questions.explanation_hi:
आधिकारिक व्याख्या (Unit 2: Industrial Location Theories):
Weber defined Material Index MI = (Weight of localized raw materials) / (Weight of finished product). If MI > 1 (weight-losing industry like iron smelting or sugar milling), the optimal plant location is pulled toward the raw material source; if MI ≤ 1, it locates at the market.

questions.question_en: In K. J. Kansky's (1963) Graph Theory analysis of transport networks, if a planar network graph has V = 10 vertices (nodes), E = 15 edges (links), and G = 1 connected sub-graph, what are the values of the Beta index (β = E / V) and the Cyclomatic number (μ = E − V + G)?
questions.question_hi:
[Unit 4: Transport Networks & Connectivity]
In K. J. Kansky's (1963) Graph Theory analysis of transport networks, if a planar network graph has V = 10 vertices (nodes), E = 15 edges (links), and G = 1 connected sub-graph, what are the values of the Beta index (β = E / V) and the Cyclomatic number (μ = E − V + G)?
questions.explanation_en: Beta index β = E / V = 15 / 10 = 1.5 (values > 1 indicate a complex connected network with multiple circuits). Cyclomatic number μ = E − V + G = 15 − 10 + 1 = 6 fundamental circuits.
questions.explanation_hi:
आधिकारिक व्याख्या (Unit 4: Transport Networks & Connectivity):

questions.question_en: In Kansky's planar transport graph indices, the Gamma index (γ), which measures the ratio of observed edges (E) to the maximum possible number of edges in a planar graph with V ≥ 3 vertices, is given by:
questions.question_hi:
[Unit 4: Transport Networks & Connectivity]
In Kansky's planar transport graph indices, the Gamma index (γ), which measures the ratio of observed edges (E) to the maximum possible number of edges in a planar graph with V ≥ 3 vertices, is given by:
questions.explanation_en: In a planar graph (where edges do not cross without a node), adding a new vertex adds at most 3 new edges, so E_max = 3(V − 2). Hence γ_planar = E / [3(V − 2)], while α_planar = (E − V + G) / (2V − 5).
questions.explanation_hi:
आधिकारिक व्याख्या (Unit 4: Transport Networks & Connectivity):
In a planar graph (where edges do not cross without a node), adding a new vertex adds at most 3 new edges, so E_max = 3(V − 2). Hence γ_planar = E / [3(V − 2)], while α_planar = (E − V + G) / (2V − 5).
